title: Defence workers: the Bharatiya Pratiraksha Mazdoor Sangh
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Ordnance factories, corporatisation and the question of national security.
body:
The **Bharatiya Pratiraksha Mazdoor Sangh (BPMS)** is the BMS federation of defence civilian employees, including those in ordnance factories, defence production units and other establishments under the Ministry of Defence. Its work is easier to understand if one looks at the single biggest structural change in the sector in recent decades: the end of the Ordnance Factory Board and the creation of seven new companies in 2021.

## Who are defence civilian workers?

Most people picture the armed forces when they think of defence. Behind them is a large civilian workforce: skilled and semi-skilled workers who turn out ammunition, vehicles, clothing, optical equipment and many other items, along with the technicians, clerks and supervisors who keep those factories running. For many decades the ordnance factories, managed by the Ordnance Factory Board (OFB) with its headquarters in Kolkata, formed the backbone of this production system. These employees were central government servants. Their pay, leave, medical facilities, promotions and pensions followed central government rules, and that is the reason the unions that represent them pay such close attention to any change in their legal status.

BPMS is the BMS-affiliated union in this field. It describes itself as a union of civilian workers in factories and establishments under the Defence Ministry, and it works alongside other recognised federations of defence employees. In disputes over the future of the factories, these organisations have often acted jointly, even though they belong to different central trade union families.

## The 2021 restructuring: what happened

On **16 June 2021** the Union Cabinet approved a plan to restructure the ordnance factories. As reported at the time, the Ministry of Defence announced on 17 June that the operating units of the OFB, together with parachute and opto-electronics units, would be split into **seven government-owned companies**. The Board itself was dissolved with effect from **1 October 2021**, and the new companies were formally launched on **15 October 2021**.

The seven defence public sector undertakings (DPSUs) are:

- Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited
- Armoured Vehicles Nigam Limited
- Gliders India Limited
- India Optel Limited
- Munitions India Limited
- Troop Comforts Limited
- Yantra India Limited

Together they took over the **41 production units** that had been run by the OFB. The government's stated purpose was to give the units greater autonomy, to improve efficiency and accountability, and to make them better able to compete for orders. Unions saw the matter differently, and the disagreement is the source of most of the issues described below.

## What it meant for the employees

The Ministry of Defence explained the arrangement for employees in a written reply to Parliament in February 2022. Employees of the former OFB in the production units, and in the identified non-production units, were placed on what is called **deemed deputation** to the seven new corporations. The initial period was **two years from 1 October 2021**. During that time they remained subject to the rules that apply to central government servants on matters such as pay scales, allowances, leave, medical facilities and career progression. The reply also said that the government would continue to bear pension liabilities for retirees and for existing employees, and that those recruited on or after 1 January 2004 are covered by the National Pension System.

Deemed deputation was not meant to be permanent. In August 2023 the government approved an **extension of one year from 1 October 2023** for Group A, B and C employees. The same order required each of the seven companies to finalise service rules for absorbed employees and, within that one-year period, to **seek options** from employees on whether they wished to be permanently absorbed into the company concerned. This is the stage the original post refers to when it says that employees "had options on terms of service". For a worker, the choice carries real weight. Permanent absorption means moving from the status of a central government employee to that of an employee of a company, with the service rules, promotion structure and long-term protections of that company. Many employees want to understand those rules fully before they choose.

## The numbers behind the change

The older figures are worth remembering. The OFB workforce has been described as running to roughly eighty thousand employees. The Ministry's February 2022 reply put the order book of the seven new corporations at **115 contracts worth about Rs 79,834 crore** at that time. These figures show two things: the sector is large in terms of both people and money, and the government's argument for restructuring is tied to the objective of securing orders and delivering them on time. Unions, for their part, point to the fact that the factories had already been producing for the armed forces for many years.

## Issues that defence unions raise

The concerns raised by BPMS and other defence employee federations may be grouped as follows.

- **Service conditions and pensions.** Workers want a clear and written guarantee that pay, allowances, promotion avenues and pension benefits will not be diluted after absorption, and that those who joined before 2004 will not lose the benefits tied to their original status.
- **Option letters.** The documents through which employees are asked to choose absorption must, in the unions' view, be transparent and must explain the consequences in plain language. In September 2025 BPMS joined AIDEF, INTUC and CDRA in a campaign of pamphlet distribution and general meetings at ordnance factories, covering corporatisation, service conditions and the approaching option letters.
- **Recruitment and vacancies.** Unfilled posts add to the workload of those in service and weaken the capacity of the factories.
- **Indigenisation and public sector strength.** The argument is that production for national security is best kept in public hands and strengthened with orders, investment and modern technology.
- **Wages and allowances.** Defence employees look for pay and allowances in line with central government rules, along with timely revision of incentives and bonuses.

## The BMS position

BMS has taken a consistent line: defence is a national responsibility, and defence workers are part of the national security chain. In August 2019, when the government's corporatisation plan was first met with a strike notice and work stoppages, the BMS national executive resolution criticised the push for disinvestment of public sector units and said privatisation in such sectors would harm the national interest; BPMS joined the strike action along with two other federations. BMS has also stressed that, whatever the structure chosen, the interests of employees must be protected and that sensitive areas should not be handed over to private hands.

At the same time, BMS tries to keep the discussion constructive. It prefers negotiation, representation and peaceful agitation to confrontation, and it has worked alongside other defence federations on the issue. That method follows the founder's view that demands should be firm but that the method should always be lawful and constructive.

## What remains to be done

Three questions stay open. First, will the service rules and the option process give every worker a fair and informed choice? Second, will the new companies receive enough orders and investment to remain secure, so that absorbed employees are not left worse off in the long run? Third, how will the government and the unions keep their channels of dialogue open? Answers will emerge in the coming years, and BPMS will continue to represent its members in the discussions that follow.

## A reminder

When a soldier fires, he relies on a worker who made the weapon. The worker deserves the same respect as the soldier.
